lesson.title: Mass Number: Counting the Nucleus's Heavy Particles
lesson.summary: Mass number is the total count of protons plus neutrons in a nucleus, giving a whole-number label for how heavy a particular atom is.
lesson.body:
Atomic number tells you how many protons an atom has, but it says nothing about neutrons, and neutrons contribute nearly as much mass to an atom as protons do. Mass number fills that gap. Mass number, given the symbol A, is defined as the sum of the number of protons and the number of neutrons in a nucleus: A equals Z plus N, where Z is atomic number, the proton count, and N is the neutron count. Unlike atomic number, mass number is not a fixed property of an element, because different atoms of the same element can have different neutron counts, and therefore different mass numbers, while still sharing the same atomic number.

Mass number is always a whole number, since you cannot have a fractional proton or neutron, and it is typically written either as a superscript before an element's symbol, such as in carbon-14 written as a superscript 14 before C, or spelled out after the element name, as in uranium-238. It is important not to confuse mass number with atomic mass, which is measured in atomic mass units and includes small corrections for nuclear binding energy. Mass number is a simple particle count, an integer, while atomic mass is a measured physical quantity that is close to, but not exactly equal to, the mass number.

The relationship A equals Z plus N makes mass number calculations straightforward once you know any two of the three quantities. Take uranium-238, a commonly cited isotope. Uranium has atomic number 92, meaning every uranium atom has 92 protons. If the mass number is 238, then the neutron count is found by rearranging the equation: N equals A minus Z, so N equals 238 minus 92, which is 146 neutrons. This single isotope, uranium-238, therefore contains 92 protons and 146 neutrons packed into one nucleus, for a total of 238 nuclear particles.

A second worked example demonstrates the reverse direction. Suppose you are told an atom has 20 protons and 20 neutrons. Its atomic number is 20, identifying it as calcium, since calcium's atomic number is 20. Its mass number is the sum, 20 plus 20, which equals 40, so this atom is calcium-40, in fact the most abundant naturally occurring isotope of calcium. If instead that same calcium atom had 22 neutrons rather than 20, its mass number would be 20 plus 22, equal to 42, making it calcium-42, a different isotope of the same element, since the atomic number, and therefore the identity, has not changed.

Mass number is the essential ingredient for identifying isotopes, since two atoms of the same element with different mass numbers, and therefore different neutron counts, are by definition isotopes of each other. It also feeds directly into atomic mass, since the mass number tells you roughly, though not exactly, how many atomic mass units a given isotope weighs, with the small remaining difference explained by the binding energy that holds the nucleus together.
